reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Describes pituitary adenomas occurring in two or more members of a family in the absence of MEN1 or Carney complex
A substantial minority of cases carry germline mutations in the AIP gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance
AIP-related adenomas frequently secrete growth hormone or prolactin and often present as gigantism or acromegaly
Onset is characteristically young, sometimes in childhood or adolescence, and tumours tend to be large and invasive
AIP-related somatotroph tumours may respond less well to somatostatin analogue therapy than typical sporadic tumours
Screening of at-risk relatives allows earlier detection while adenomas are smaller and more treatable
The absence of parathyroid or pancreatic involvement helps distinguish it from MEN1
reference.pathophysiology: AIP encodes the aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein, which functions as a tumour suppressor within pituitary cells. Germline loss-of-function mutations predispose to adenoma formation, typically after loss of the second allele in a pituitary cell consistent with a tumour-suppressor mechanism. The resulting tumours arise most often from growth hormone- or prolactin-secreting lineages, producing hormone excess and mass effects. Incomplete penetrance means not all carriers develop tumours, but those who do tend to present young with larger, more aggressive adenomas than sporadic cases.
additionalInvestigations: Pituitary hormone profile including growth hormone, IGF-1 and prolactin
Dynamic testing such as oral glucose suppression when acromegaly is suspected
Dedicated pituitary MRI to characterise tumour size and invasion
Visual field assessment where the tumour approaches the optic chiasm
Molecular genetic testing of AIP in the index case and at-risk relatives
redFlags: Visual field loss or cranial nerve involvement from a large invasive adenoma
Pituitary apoplexy presenting with sudden headache and visual disturbance
Rapid tumour growth or hormone excess in a young patient
Features of hypopituitarism from compression of normal pituitary tissue
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on tumour size, invasiveness and treatment response; AIP-related tumours are often larger and less responsive to medical therapy, so early detection through family screening improves the likelihood of successful control.
pitfalls: Assuming a young patient with acromegaly or gigantism has purely sporadic disease
Overlooking a family history of pituitary tumours that points to an inherited predisposition
Failing to offer genetic testing and surveillance to relatives of AIP mutation carriers
Expecting a standard response to somatostatin analogues in AIP-related somatotroph tumours
